Your site publishes two small data files. Ten lines, explained. This is the route for a section of an existing site.

2. Run a newsroom like this one. The newsroom's repository is public: the pages, the build, the sync, the gate, the engineering board. Fork it, point it at this host, change the words. 3. Pilot it with us. For a publisher who wants to try the whole thing, meter, personas, lists, the vault, on a part of their site with their own payment link and lane, and to learn with us from what readers do. Write to agent@riskmandate.ai (an agent reads first; a person answers) or open an issue.

One line that pins the release you load, and a copy of its manifest. Taking a release.

You keep your readers' trust in a concrete form: their data never reaches you unless they send it, and when they do it arrives encrypted to a key only you hold. You keep the money, through your own payment link. You keep the site you have.

The code lives on one host, in one directory per release, and a release is never changed after it is published. The pages that run it live wherever the newsroom lives. Everything about a reader stays with the page.

<path> is the path the file had in the newsroom's repository, so the move was a prefix rewrite and nothing else; reshaping the paths is a later phase. The meter's own component versions nest inside the release unchanged. manifest.json lists every path with its bytes and SHA-256, and which files differ from the newsroom's bytes and why. releases.json lists the releases.

GitHub Pages serves every file with access-control-allow-origin: *. That is what an ES module import from another origin needs, and what the component base needs when it fetches a component's .tpl and .css beside its .js through import.meta.url. Classic <script src> tags (the vendored vault library) need nothing. The live check after every deploy fails if the header is missing.

The reader's state. localStorage and sessionStorage belong to the page's origin, not the script's. sgit.meter.v1 stays on the newsroom whichever host serves the meter. This is the property the move depended on, and a test records it.

The site's data. The meter fetches the article feed and the contact file from cfg.root on the page; the reading list fetches articles/ids.json from where the page says. Nothing is fetched from this host but code.

The addresses. The Stripe return page, /for/#…, /persona/<id>/, /.well-known/sgit-subscribe.json are the newsroom's; pages do not move to this host, and could not, because another origin has another origin's storage.

Three files locate the site's root to link to pages and fetch data: the vault pane, search and ask. In the newsroom they did it from their own URL; on another host that would be this host. They now read <html data-root="…">, the path from the page to the site root, which every newsroom page carries ("" at the root, "../" one level down). A page that imports them needs the attribute. The code they load (the vault library) they still find from their own URL.

A consuming site writes the release into one file and generates every URL from it. The newsroom's is admin/build/api.json; its admin/build/api.py --repoint rewrites every page, its gate (check 14) refuses a relative, unpinned or unlisted reader-file reference, and check 13 holds the frozen meter copies it still serves to the manifest's bytes. A rollback is the previous release in that file and one run. Taking a release.

No page sets one yet (finding R10). When one is added, script-src and connect-src include https://api.newsroom.sgit.ai; frame-ancestors cannot be set in a meta tag, so framing protection needs a host that sets headers, which GitHub Pages is not. The order of work in the brief is: load scripts as modules instead of fetched text through eval, then the meta policy, then decide on a layer in front.

Three files could not move unchanged, because they located the site root from their own URL: assets/vault-pane/vault-pane.js, assets/search/search.js, assets/search/ask.js. Each now takes the site root from the page (data-root) and keeps a second root, its own, for the code it loads. The manifest records each with its before-hash and the reason, and tools/release.py refuses any other difference from the newsroom's bytes. The proof.

Every file is served from this host at a versioned path that is never edited after it is published, and every release has a manifest of hashes. You pin a release; a rollback is one line.

Three pieces in the page: the element where the charge happens, the config, and the import. The element's kind is the price class; the config is the same on every page of a site, so write it once in your build.

Prices are in pence (or the smallest unit of symbol). start is the opening credit. This page is for the person who has to say yes or no. It is written so that nothing on it needs to be taken on trust: every number is read from a record in the repository, every finding is a public issue, every file has a hash on the live host, and the move that put the code here was proved byte for byte.

There is no server of ours: the reader code is static files on a host that cannot run code, and the pages that use it are static too. The reader's state (balance, history, personas, lists, notes) lives in the browser's storage on the newsroom's origin, and optionally in an encrypted vault whose keys derive from the reader's passkey and which the newsroom cannot open. Money moves through a Stripe Payment Link the newsroom owns; a return page credits the balance once per payment reference. Anything a reader sends (a share, a subscription, a note) is encrypted in the browser to a published key and appended to a write-only lane in a vault.

Nine channels, each listed with what, when and who sees it, on state, inputs and outputs, read from the map. In short: the page's own origin for files; POST of an encrypted envelope to the lane when the reader presses Send; navigation to Stripe when they press Top up; GET of ciphertext from the wire's vault; a postMessage ready signal if a page is framed; the clipboard and a download at the reader's command. The tests record the hosts a page contacted and fail on any other.

The security model on the newsroom (meter/security.html) accepts four things a server would prevent, because there is no server by design: the return page credits any session id; the reader can edit their own balance; the names in a reading list are whatever the link says; a page is charged by the deepest point reached. The review's job was to prove those are the only gaps.

Before the code moved here it was mapped and reviewed line by line, the way a fractal semantic graph is read: every file, every control a reader can click, type or pay, every input and output, every contract, then every function the findings name. The findings are issues 1 to 18 in the repository, labelled by phase, area and severity. Where a finding can be pinned, a test records the behaviour as it is today, so that the fix is a visible change to a test. The three a security evaluator will want first:

No Content-Security-Policy on any page (R10, high). The pages' loader runs fetched scripts through eval, and GitHub Pages sets no headers, so frame-ancestors cannot be set. The fix is a phase-5 change: load scripts as modules, then a meta CSP; framing protection needs a host that sets headers.
Payment references unbounded and unchecked (R14, low) and restore() trusts a file's fields (R2, low): the exposure is a file someone sent the reader to restore.
Production reader data goes to hosts named dev (R5): a naming decision for the operator, listed so that nobody is surprised.
The full table, with the test that pins each and the proposed change.
Third-party scripts on the reader pages: none. The build fails if one appears (the brief's rule).
One vendored library, the vault library that runs the SG/Send host, pinned at a version and never edited here; its twelve files are hashed in VENDOR.md and the test checks them.
Every release is a manifest of paths, bytes and SHA-256; the live host is checked against it after every deploy (tools/live_check.py), because green does not mean live.
Nothing is edited in place. A release directory, once published, is frozen; CI recomputes every hash in every manifest on every commit.

This code lived in the newsroom's repository until 13 October 2026. Moving it to a host of its own was done as a pure refactoring, and proved: of 74 files, 60 hash exactly as they did before, and the three that differ do so by the lines that located the site root from the script's own address, each recorded in the manifest with its before-hash and the reason; of 597 pages on the newsroom, 593 normalise to what they were. The proof, with the report it was written from.

Every commit: syntax, the manifest, a build that is the same bytes twice, and the tests in Chromium, WebKit and Firefox against the newsroom's real pages, in about four minutes. Every push to main: a tag, the Pages deploy, and the live check. A pull request needs a person and an agent reviewer. The runs.

The newsroom's gate does the equivalent on its side: every page must load the reader code from the pinned release, by a URL that is in the manifest, and never by a relative path. Its source is public too.

You know the problem. A paywall turns a reader away at the door; a free site pays nothing back; a subscription asks for a commitment before the first paragraph. This is a third thing, running on a live site since October 2026: a reader walks in with a small credit, a meter charges by how far they read, they pay after, and what they pay is set by what they thought of it. Around it, a newsroom that is theirs: personas, picks, lists they can send in a link, an account that travels with them, and none of it on a server of ours.
Everything on this page is running at newsroom.sgit.ai. Open any article and watch the balance in the top bar; the reading account shows what you spent and why. It is a working instance, not a demo.

£5 of credit to begin. An article costs 5p, a new one 10p, charged by the deepest point reached. Rate it at the foot and the price moves: excellent is double, not useful is free. Declining refunds the page.
A founder, a journalist, a security lead, a builder, a board member. Each has a starting reading list and picks that follow what they keep and reject. A link can open the site as one.
Every article has a number that never changes. A reading list is a link with the numbers in it, from you to a named reader, with a note. Nothing is stored anywhere but the link.
A passkey opens an encrypted vault that carries the reading account between a phone and a laptop. The newsroom never holds a key and cannot read it.
A reader marks a page done, wrong, more like this, or writes to the newsroom; the notes travel in their vault and arrive encrypted in a lane the newsroom reads.
Stories agents gather into a vault, read live in the browser, filtered by the reader's lens, with what is new since their last visit.
The money. A reader tops up through a Stripe Payment Link you own; the return page credits their balance. No card data touches your site.
The formats. Article numbers, persona links, the reading-list grammar, the share envelope: published contracts your readers and their agents can rely on, and that other newsrooms can share.
The relationship. Shares and subscriptions arrive encrypted to a key only you hold, in a write-only lane; notes from the pane arrive the same way, with the page and the reader's words.
The site you have. Static pages, any host. The reader code is a handful of files pinned from this host.

Reader data. The balance, the history, the personas, the lists and the notes live in the reader's browser, and in their own vault if they choose one. There is no reader database because there is no server.
Keys. The vault's keys are derived from the reader's passkey; the newsroom reads a lane with a read key the reader hands over, and nothing else.
A dependency on us. The code is Apache 2.0, every release is a directory of files with a manifest of hashes, and a rollback is one line.
Your pages, wherever they are hosted. The meter is a custom element and a JSON config on each page; the balance chip sits in your navigation. Ten lines.
An article feed (titles, dates, topics, teasers) for the picks, and a numbers file that gives every article a stable number. The newsroom's build writes both; yours can too. The contracts.
A Stripe Payment Link for the top-up, returning to your account page. Until it is set, the site says so and no money moves.
Shares, subscriptions and notes arrive in an encrypted vault on an SG/Send host, drained by a person or an agent with your key. Without it, the meter still runs; the reader just cannot write back.
One line names the release you load from this host; a manifest lists every file's hash; a rollback is the previous line. How.

The site that runs this says so on its own what runs, what is designed page, and the review here lists it as findings. In short: the balance lives in the reader's browser, so a reader can edit their own credit, and the return page credits a payment reference without verifying it; both are accepted and written down in the security model. No page sets a Content-Security-Policy yet. The vault hosts the live site uses are named dev. Shares from the newsroom are still labelled with the site the code came from. Each is an open issue with a proposed change, and each will be a visible change to a test when it is fixed.

A release is a directory that is never changed after it is on dev, the default branch. The tree is always exactly the release the version file names, or the check fails.

Until phase 4 of the brief is finished (the refactoring with every test passing, and the adversarial exercise), the served files change only as a new release, each change with a test that fails without it and a reason in the pull request. Edit under the served paths (assets/, for/, wire/, passkey/); if the file is one of the meter's, it is a new component version at a new path, never an edit of v1.4.1. Run the tests in the three engines against the newsroom checkout (running the tests).
tools/version.json holds two numbers and a date, all from the file, never the clock:

version, the repository's version. Every change that lands on dev is a new one, in small increments: a patch for a small change (v0.2.1, v0.2.2, ...), a minor for a new capability. The deploy tags it, and refuses a version that is already a tag or not above the latest. CI on a branch fails when the version is not above dev's.
release, the latest cut of the reader code: releases/<release>/, what the consuming sites pin. It changes only when a served file changes; then it is set to the new version and cut.

Add the version's line to site/data/versions.json (newest first); the build refuses a version without one, and /versions/ shows them all. A new page needs its link-preview card: python3 site/og.py draws one into site/og/ for every page that has none (commit it; the gate fails a page without one).

cut refuses to write over an existing release directory, refuses a release that is not the repository's version, and refuses a file that differs from the newsroom's bytes unless CHANGED_FROM_NEWSROOM records why. Write a release's note at site/releases/v0.2.3.md.

A reader presses Send; their browser encrypts a small message to your public key and appends it to a lane you own. The site never sees it. You read the lane with your key, by hand or with an agent.

A key pair. An RSA key whose public half is published; the private half stays with whoever (or whichever agent) reads the lane. The envelope is RSA-OAEP-SHA256 wrapping an AES-256-GCM key (the sgit hybrid envelope v2).

A vault with an append lane on an SG/Send host, with an append token that lets a browser write and nothing else. The newsroom's lane is on dev.send.sgraph.ai (named dev; finding R5 asks the operator to say whether that is production).

The browser recomputes the fingerprint from the PEM before encrypting, so a swapped key is refused. The newsroom's own file is here; it is still labelled with the site the code came from (finding R4), which the move makes possible to fix.

A subscription is an .eml with the address and a consent line; a share is the reader's summary and their data as JSON (balance, spent, reads, personas, topics, log; never a payment reference), with headers X-SGit-Form, X-SGit-Reply-To, X-SGit-Name, X-SGit-Subscribe, X-SGit-Page. A note from the vault pane arrives in the reader's own lane, whose read key they hand over, with the page, their words and the phrase they selected.

Before anything moved, everything a reader does on newsroom.sgit.ai was mapped: every file, every control a reader can click, type or pay, every input, every place data leaves the browser, every contract. Source code is layers within layers, each a graph with its own vocabulary, and a review should read a change at every one: that is the method in Code review as a fractal semantic graph. Here the layers are: the site a reader opens; the pages written for the reader code; the views, controls, inputs and outputs on them; the files that run them and the contracts between them; and inside each file the functions the findings name. It is an API with no server. "API" here means client-side: the components, formats and contracts a browser runs. The host serves files over GitHub Pages and receives nothing; the reader's balance, personas and vault keys stay in the page's own storage, as they always have.

A site pins a release, and a release is never edited. The newsroom names one release in a file and copies its manifest; its gate fails the build on any reference that is not pinned, not in the manifest, or relative. A change to the code is a new directory, never an edit of an old one.

The brief for this is the owner's article Go slow to go fast, and the short version is that the reader code had been written the way an explorer writes: fast, in the same tree as everything else, changed in the same commit as an article. That was right while it was being invented. It stops being right once other people depend on it. A change to the meter was a change to the site with no version of its own; a review had no boundary to stand on; and a second site, sgit.ai, which carries the same meter, had no way to say which meter it meant.

Before and after the move. Before, one repository held newsroom.sgit.ai's 738 pages and, beside them, the code they run, loaded by a relative address. A page that uses the API does three things. It names a release: the newsroom's is one line in admin/build/api.json. It copies that release's manifest.json, so its own build knows the hash of every file it may load. And it loads the code by its full address:

The rule of the move was identical paths under a versioned prefix. A file that was at assets/search/search.js on the newsroom is at /v0.2.5/assets/search/search.js on the host, so moving a page to the host is a rewrite of a prefix, and checking it is a comparison of hashes rather than a reading of diffs.

Where the code runs is the part that matters for a reader. A script loaded from another host still runs on the page's origin, so the meter's balance, the personas, the reading list and the vault's keys are kept in newsroom.sgit.ai's browser storage, exactly where they were. The API host is GitHub Pages: it serves files with access-control-allow-origin: *, which is what lets a module from one host be imported by a page on another, and it has no way to receive anything. Before the release I proved that model with a page on one origin importing the meter from another and finding its storage where it should be.

Three files could not move unchanged, and they are the only code changes the move made. vault-pane.js, search.js and ask.js found the site's root from their own address, which on a second host is the wrong site. Every page: 735 of 738 the same once the chrome, the version stamps and the code's new address are normalised; the other three are the versions table, the engineering index and the search index, which change because a release was made.

A move like this is easy to claim and hard to check by reading, so the check is a script. tools/prove_move.py takes the newsroom before the move and the newsroom after it, and compares three things: every served file against its bytes before, by hash; the frozen copies in all three trees; and every one of the 738 pages, after normalising the parts that are allowed to change, the site's chrome, the version stamps, and the address of the code. The other thirteen versions changed the website, the tests or the pipeline and left the served files as they were. Each has a line on the versions page, and the feed carries them for a site that wants to know when the next release lands.

The host also serves the site that explains it, at its root, beside the release directories: api.newsroom.sgit.ai. It has a door for each kind of reader. Publishers and editors get the case and the cost of adopting it. Developers get a quick start with the real config. Evaluators get the trust boundaries, what leaves the browser, the findings, the supply chain and how to verify the live host themselves. Agents get the brief, and every page has a markdown twin, a block for agents, and a place in llms.txt, because the people you talk to work with agents.

The instruction for the website was feature parity with newsroom.sgit.ai before anything switches, and that is what versions v0.2.2 to v0.2.13 did. It wears the newsroom's five themes, with the newsroom's token file and picker copied byte for byte and a test that says so. The bar has the newsroom's shape, eight groups with their pages under them. The footer carries the same disclosure and network line. Every page has a link-preview card. There is a feed. And search, which on the newsroom is the API's search component over the newsroom's index, is here the same component, loaded from the host's own release, over an index the website's build writes in the same format. The site uses what it serves.

The site has its own gate, site/check.py, modelled on the newsroom's: every reference resolves, every page has its canonical address, its chrome, its card and its twin, the sitemap and the llms files agree with the tree, and nothing shaped like a key is published. Its first run found five links on the review pages to map data that had never been published. A test in three engines holds the website to the newsroom's bar: every theme token defined in all five themes, no colour written outside a token, 4.5:1 contrast for text in every theme, the bar on one row from 1280 pixels and nothing wider than the screen at any width down to 360.

In all, 764 checks in fifteen tests. Continuous integration runs all fifteen in Chromium and the nine that need no Chromium-only protocol in WebKit and Firefox, on every commit. Two of the sixteen versions exist because one test was unsteady: the pin for a finding where a broken persona leaves the personas page unusable. The first fix accepted both forms the page takes, blank or failed; the second, which held, made the test put the broken persona into the saved state on the page it measures, so the meter's own save on the page before could not overwrite it.

The host is live, three releases are published, and the website has what the newsroom's has. What has not happened yet is the switch: newsroom.sgit.ai still serves its own copy of the reader code. The newsroom's side of the move, its v0.13.0, is written and waiting on a branch, pinned to v0.2.0, with its gate passing and its pages proved. It was held on purpose. The instruction was to reach parity first and switch after, in phases, and while it waited the newsroom kept shipping: its dev is now 33 releases past the commit the switch was built on.
Fold the newsroom's new work into a new cut. Whatever reader code changed in those 33 releases becomes the next release of the API, cut from the commit that will pin it, and the proof is run again.
Switch in phases. The newsroom takes the release a group of pages at a time, beginning with the pages that carry least, each step proved by hash before the next.
Environments. A pre-production host for a release before the live site pins it, which the brief asks for and which has not been built.
sgit.ai pins the same release, so the two sites that carry the meter mean the same meter.
Phase three and four of the brief: the refactoring, with every test passing, and the adversarial review, starting from the eighteen findings.

newsroom.sgit.ai does not use the host yet. Every number about the newsroom's pages describes the switch as built and proved on its branch, against the newsroom at v0.12.50; it is not live, and the newsroom has moved since.

The same bytes, not the same behaviour, is what the proof proves. Identical files and pages imply the same behaviour for everything that runs from them; the three changed files are covered by the tests, not by the hash.

Five of the sixteen tags are missing. The deploy's token is refused a tag on a commit whose workflow files differ from the current ones, so v0.2.1 to v0.2.4 and v0.2.6 are in the history and on the versions page but need a person to push their tags.
The eighteen findings are open. They are pinned by tests as the behaviour is today; fixing them is phase three and four, and each fix will be a deliberate change to the test that pinned it.

The check counts are one run's. They are counted from one run in Chromium on 16 October; WebKit and Firefox run fewer tests, and a test's count changes when the newsroom's pages or the vault's content do.
"No server" is about the API. The reader code talks to other hosts, the vault host and the payment provider among them, as the evaluators' page lists with what each sees; the API itself is files.
If you run a site that could use the meter, the lists or the vault pane, or you want to review the code before it is refactored, write to agent@riskmandate.ai or open an issue.
